# Mechanistic models and pharmacometrics {#sec-b15}

<!-- page-provenance:start -->
::: {.page-provenance}
*R. Heller · Date: 2026-04-12 · Last changed: 2026-11-09*
:::
<!-- page-provenance:end -->



::: {.callout-note appearance="simple" icon=false}
## At a glance

**Guiding question:** Which sampling times make it possible to separate clearance from volume?\
**For:** clinical pharmacology trainees, doctoral students planning sampling schedules, reviewers of
pharmacokinetic analyses ·
**Prerequisites:** exponential functions and logarithms, the idea of a likelihood (@sec-b16 uses it as well),
repeated measurements per person (@sec-b13)\
**In the course:** [W6 · Pharmacometrics, forecasting and simulation](https://cttir.github.io/clinical-data-science-in-r-course/lessons/w6-pharmacometrics-forecasting-simulation.html) ·
**Data:** synthetic, virtual parameters only (generated in the chapter) ·
**Core reading time:** about 11 minutes
:::

::: {.callout-warning title="Virtual parameters only"}
Every dose, volume and clearance in this chapter is a *virtual* model input for a fictitious compound. Nothing here is
a dosing recommendation, and the numbers do not describe any real drug or patient group.
:::

## Case and decision {#sec-b15-case}

A doctoral researcher in clinical pharmacology is writing the sampling section of a protocol for a fictitious
intravenous compound in injured adults. The ethics committee has asked the team to keep blood sampling to a minimum,
and the trial unit can process two samples per person. The researcher must choose the two times. A senior colleague
suggests taking both samples late, at 6 and 8 hours, "because by then the drug is evenly distributed". Another
proposes one sample shortly after the injection and one late. The protocol will fix the times for every participant,
and they cannot be changed after the first person is enrolled. Which schedule allows the clearance and the volume of
distribution to be estimated separately – and how precisely? The chapter answers with a one-compartment model and
*virtual* parameters only.

## Core reading {#sec-b15-core}

::: {.callout-important appearance="simple" icon=false}
**Core reading** · required for W6 (alternative to @sec-b18) · about 11 minutes · ends before ‘Lab’
:::



**From mass balance to a concentration curve.** A one-compartment model treats the body as one well-mixed volume. Let
A(t) be the amount of compound in the body (mg) and C(t) the plasma concentration (mg/L). The volume of distribution V
(L) links the two: C = A / V. It is a proportionality constant, not an anatomical space. The clearance CL (L/h) is the
volume of plasma cleared of the compound per hour, so the elimination rate is CL × C, in L/h × mg/L = mg/h. The mass
balance says that the amount in the body falls exactly by what is eliminated:

$$
\frac{dA}{dt} = -\,CL \cdot C = -\frac{CL}{V}\,A, \qquad A(0) = \text{dose}.
$$

The units check: (L/h) / L × mg = mg/h. After a single intravenous bolus, the solution is
C(t) = (dose / V) · exp(−(CL / V) · t). The ratio k = CL / V (1/h) is the elimination rate constant, the half-life is
ln 2 · V / CL, and the area under the curve from zero to infinity is dose / CL (mg·h/L). With the virtual values dose
= 100 mg, V = 20 L and CL = 5 L/h, the initial concentration is 5 mg/L, the
half-life 2.77 h and the AUC 20 mg·h/L.

**Two parameters, one sample.** On a logarithmic scale the curve is a straight line: ln C(t) = ln(dose / V) − k · t.
The intercept carries the volume, the slope carries the ratio CL / V. One sample, or two samples at the same time,
gives one equation for two unknowns. Panel (a) of @fig-b15-identifiability shows two virtual parameter sets that
produce exactly the same concentration at 4 h: V = 20 L with CL = 5 L/h, and V = 26 L with
CL = 4.79 L/h. A design that measures only at 4 h cannot tell them apart. This is structural
non-identifiability [@bellman1970structural]: no amount of measurement precision helps.


::: {.cell}
::: {.cell-output-display}
![Identifiability in a one-compartment model with *virtual* parameters (dose 100 mg intravenous bolus). (a) Concentration (mg/L, log scale) for two parameter sets that coincide at 4 h; symbols mark the sampling times of designs A–C. (b) Normalised sensitivity of ln C to ln V and ln CL; at t = V/CL = 4 h, a sample carries no information about V. One virtual person, no measurement error.](b15-mechanistic-models-pharmacometrics_files/figure-epub/fig-b15-identifiability-1.png){#fig-b15-identifiability fig-alt='Two panels. Panel a shows two declining straight lines on a logarithmic concentration axis from 0 to 12 hours: one for volume 20 litres and clearance 5 litres per hour, one for volume 26 litres and lower clearance. They start at different heights, cross at 4 hours and then diverge slightly. Sampling times of three designs are marked below the curves: design A at 0.5 and 8 hours, design B at 6 and 8 hours, design C at 0.5 and 1 hour. Panel b shows two straight sensitivity lines over time: the sensitivity to volume starts at minus 1 and rises, crossing zero at 4 hours; the sensitivity to clearance starts at 0 and falls steadily.'}
:::
:::


**Where a sample is informative.** Panel (b) shows the normalised sensitivities: how much ln C changes when ln V or
ln CL changes. For the volume, the sensitivity is −1 + k · t; it is zero at t = V / CL = 4 h. A sample taken then is
blind to V, given CL. For the clearance, the sensitivity is −k · t; early samples hardly inform it. The two
parameters are separated best when the samples sit at times where the two curves differ in shape, early and late.

**Two samples, four designs.** With a proportional measurement error of 10% (*assumption*), the expected standard
errors follow from these sensitivities (the Fisher information, linearised at the virtual values).
@tbl-b15-designs compares four designs. The early-and-late design A estimates both parameters to within about 7–11%.
Two late samples (design B) leave the volume uncertain by about 50%, because the intercept must be extrapolated
back over six hours. Design B is structurally identifiable, yet practically the data hardly constrain V – the
distinction between structural and practical identifiability [@raue2009structural]. Two early samples (design C) estimate the volume reasonably but the clearance hardly at all.
Two samples at the same time (design D) cannot separate the parameters at all. The simulated spread over 2,000
virtual repetitions agrees with the linearised values. Intuitively, a straight line through two points that are close
together is poorly anchored: a 10% error at either point tilts the line, and the tilt is magnified when the line is
extended back to time zero to read off the volume, or forward to infinity to obtain the area under the curve.


::: {#tbl-b15-designs .cell tbl-cap='Approximate relative standard errors (%) of V and CL for four two-sample designs, *virtual* parameters (V = 20 L, CL = 5 L/h), proportional error 10% (*assumption*). Expected: from the linearised Fisher information; simulated: standard deviation of the estimates over 2,000 virtual repetitions of one person.'}
::: {.cell-output-display}


|Design             |Sampling times (h) |       V expected|      V simulated|      CL expected|     CL simulated|
|:------------------|:------------------|----------------:|----------------:|----------------:|----------------:|
|A: early and late  |0.5 and 8          |               11|               11|                7|                7|
|B: both late       |6 and 8            |               50|               50|               22|               21|
|C: both early      |0.5 and 1          |               22|               23|               92|               85|
|D: same time twice |4 and 4            | not identifiable| not identifiable| not identifiable| not identifiable|


:::
:::


**The most important assumption.** **These standard errors hold only if the structural model is right and the
parameters are near the values used to compute them.** The best design depends on the very parameters it is meant to
estimate; the counter-check shows what happens when the clearance is lower than expected. Model-based design is
therefore local: it needs prior knowledge and should be checked across a plausible parameter range.

**Checking the arithmetic before the biology.** Most mechanistic models have no closed-form solution and are solved
numerically. Before any parameter is estimated, the lab therefore checks that the numerical solver reproduces the
analytical curve of this simple model within a tolerance fixed in advance. A closed mass balance – the amount in the
body plus the amount eliminated always equals the dose – is necessary but does not prove that the solution is
accurate.

**A baseline without a model.** With many samples per person, non-compartmental analysis (NCA) estimates the
clearance without assuming a compartment model: the AUC is computed from the measured concentrations with the
trapezoidal rule and extrapolated to infinity, and CL = dose / AUC. The lab uses it as the baseline for a virtual
person with nine samples. With two samples per person, NCA is not available, and the model carries the inference.

**Beyond one person.** Real participants differ: the clearance and the volume vary between people (interindividual
variability), and every measurement carries assay and handling error (residual variability). Population
pharmacokinetic models estimate both at once and let different people be sampled at different times
[@mould2012basic; @mould2013pk]. Automated searches over model structures, for example with genetic algorithms
[@sale2015genetic], are a further step. Neither repairs a design in which the data cannot separate the parameters.

**Question for the workshop.** The colleague's argument for late samples was that "the drug is evenly distributed by
then". In a one-compartment model this is true from the start. Which feature of a real compound would make early
samples misleading, and what would that change in the design?

## Lab {#sec-b15-lab}

The lab needs **deSolve**, **ggplot2** and **patchwork** and runs in about two seconds.

### Step 1: parameters with units


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
dose_mg <- 100           # virtual intravenous bolus (mg) – model input, not a dosing recommendation
V_l <- 20                # virtual volume of distribution (L)
CL_l_h <- 5              # virtual clearance (L/h)
k_per_h <- CL_l_h / V_l  # elimination rate constant (1/h)
sigma_log <- 0.1         # proportional measurement error, SD on the log scale (assumption)
conc_analytic <- function(t, dose = dose_mg, V = V_l, CL = CL_l_h) dose / V * exp(-CL / V * t)  # mg/L
c(C0_mg_l = dose_mg / V_l, half_life_h = log(2) * V_l / CL_l_h, AUC_mg_h_l = dose_mg / CL_l_h)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
#>     C0_mg_l half_life_h  AUC_mg_h_l 
#>    5.000000    2.772589   20.000000
```


:::
:::


### Step 2: the numerical solver against the analytical solution

The model is written as a mass balance with two states: the amount in the body (A) and the cumulative amount
eliminated (E). Before running the solver, the tolerance is fixed: the largest relative deviation from the analytical
solution at the output times must not exceed 10^−4^. This is a thousand times smaller than the assumed 10%
measurement error and below the precision of three significant digits used for reporting, so solver error cannot
change any conclusion.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
library(deSolve)
pk_rhs <- function(t, state, parms) {
  with(as.list(c(state, parms)), {
    conc <- A / V                                  # mg/L
    list(c(A = -CL * conc,                         # mg/h leaving the body
           E = CL * conc))                         # mg/h arriving in the eliminated pool
  })
}
times <- seq(0, 24, by = 0.25)                     # output grid (h)
state0 <- c(A = dose_mg, E = 0)
parms <- c(CL = CL_l_h, V = V_l)
solve_with <- function(method, ...) ode(y = state0, times = times, func = pk_rhs, parms = parms, method = method, ...)
solutions <- list(
  `lsoda, rtol = atol = 1e-8` = solve_with("lsoda", rtol = 1e-8, atol = 1e-8),
  `lsoda, defaults (1e-6)` = solve_with("lsoda"),
  `rk4, fixed step 0.25 h` = solve_with("rk4"),
  `Euler, fixed step 0.25 h` = solve_with("euler"))
tolerance <- 1e-4
reference <- conc_analytic(times)
solver_check <- data.frame(
  solver = names(solutions),
  max_relative_error = sapply(solutions, function(s) max(abs(s[, "A"] / V_l - reference) / reference)),
  max_mass_balance_error_mg = sapply(solutions, function(s) max(abs(s[, "A"] + s[, "E"] - dose_mg))))
solver_check$passes <- solver_check$max_relative_error <= tolerance
rownames(solver_check) <- NULL
solver_check
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
#>                      solver max_relative_error max_mass_balance_error_mg passes
#> 1 lsoda, rtol = atol = 1e-8       4.464623e-10              8.526513e-14   TRUE
#> 2    lsoda, defaults (1e-6)       2.921983e-08              7.105427e-14   TRUE
#> 3    rk4, fixed step 0.25 h       8.037602e-07              4.263256e-14   TRUE
#> 4  Euler, fixed step 0.25 h       1.777395e-01              2.842171e-14  FALSE
```


:::

```{.r .cell-code}
stopifnot(solver_check$passes[1:3],                        # adaptive and rk4 solutions within tolerance
          !solver_check$passes[4],                         # the check detects the inadequate Euler step
          all(solver_check$max_mass_balance_error_mg < 1e-8))  # mass is conserved by every method
```
:::


All four methods conserve mass, yet the Euler solution deviates by up to
17.8% from the analytical curve. A closed mass balance is necessary,
not sufficient; only the comparison with an independent reference reveals the error. The adaptive solver **lsoda**
[@soetaert2010desolve; @petzold1983automatic] passes with both tolerance settings.

### Step 3: structural identifiability at a single time


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
V_alt <- 26                                          # a second virtual volume (L)
CL_alt <- uniroot(function(cl) conc_analytic(4, V = V_alt, CL = cl) - conc_analytic(4),
                  interval = c(0.1, 20))$root        # clearance that gives the same C at 4 h
c(CL_alt_l_h = CL_alt, C4_set1 = conc_analytic(4), C4_set2 = conc_analytic(4, V = V_alt, CL = CL_alt),
  C05_set1 = conc_analytic(0.5), C05_set2 = conc_analytic(0.5, V = V_alt, CL = CL_alt))
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
#> CL_alt_l_h    C4_set1    C4_set2   C05_set1   C05_set2 
#>   4.794632   1.839397   1.839397   4.412485   3.507380
```


:::

```{.r .cell-code}
stopifnot(abs(conc_analytic(4) - conc_analytic(4, V = V_alt, CL = CL_alt)) < 1e-8,
          abs(conc_analytic(0.5) / conc_analytic(0.5, V = V_alt, CL = CL_alt) - 1) > 0.1)  # an early sample separates them
```
:::


### Step 4: expected precision of each design

For a log-normal error with standard deviation σ, the covariance of the estimates of (ln V, ln CL) is approximately
σ² (SᵀS)⁻¹, where each row of S holds the sensitivities d ln C / d ln V = −1 + k·t and d ln C / d ln CL = −k·t at one
sampling time. The diagonal gives the squared standard errors on the log scale, which are approximately relative
standard errors. A design whose matrix S has rank below 2 is not identifiable.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
sens_log <- function(t, V = V_l, CL = CL_l_h) cbind(lnV = -1 + CL / V * t, lnCL = -CL / V * t)
expected_se <- function(t, V = V_l, CL = CL_l_h, sigma = sigma_log) {
  S <- sens_log(t, V, CL)
  if (qr(S)$rank < 2) return(c(lnV = Inf, lnCL = Inf))  # structurally non-identifiable
  sqrt(diag(sigma^2 * solve(crossprod(S))))
}
designs <- data.frame(label = c("A", "B", "C", "D"), t1 = c(0.5, 6, 0.5, 4), t2 = c(8, 8, 1, 4),
                      description = c("early and late", "both late", "both early", "same time twice"))
# Simulation check: 2,000 virtual repetitions of one person per design, two log concentrations each
simulate_design <- function(t1, t2, n_sim = 2000, V = V_l, CL = CL_l_h) {
  if (t1 == t2) return(c(lnV = NA, lnCL = NA, share_invalid = NA))
  y1 <- log(conc_analytic(t1, V = V, CL = CL)) + rnorm(n_sim, 0, sigma_log)
  y2 <- log(conc_analytic(t2, V = V, CL = CL)) + rnorm(n_sim, 0, sigma_log)
  k_hat <- (y1 - y2) / (t2 - t1)                       # slope of the log-linear line
  V_hat <- dose_mg / exp(y1 + k_hat * t1)              # back-extrapolated intercept
  CL_hat <- k_hat * V_hat
  ok <- CL_hat > 0                                     # a negative slope gives no valid clearance
  c(lnV = sd(log(V_hat)), lnCL = sd(log(CL_hat[ok])), share_invalid = mean(!ok))
}
set.seed(15151)
expected <- t(mapply(function(a, b) expected_se(c(a, b)), designs$t1, designs$t2))
simulated <- t(mapply(simulate_design, designs$t1, designs$t2))
pct <- function(x) ifelse(is.finite(x), cdsr_number(100 * x, 0), "not identifiable")
design_table <- data.frame(
  Design = paste(designs$label, designs$description, sep = ": "),
  `Sampling times (h)` = paste(designs$t1, "and", designs$t2),
  `V expected` = pct(expected[, "lnV"]), `V simulated` = pct(simulated[, "lnV"]),
  `CL expected` = pct(expected[, "lnCL"]), `CL simulated` = pct(simulated[, "lnCL"]),
  check.names = FALSE)
design_table
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
#>               Design Sampling times (h)       V expected      V simulated
#> 1  A: early and late          0.5 and 8               11               11
#> 2       B: both late            6 and 8               50               50
#> 3      C: both early          0.5 and 1               22               23
#> 4 D: same time twice            4 and 4 not identifiable not identifiable
#>        CL expected     CL simulated
#> 1                7                7
#> 2               22               21
#> 3               92               85
#> 4 not identifiable not identifiable
```


:::

```{.r .cell-code}
stopifnot(
  all(abs(simulated[1:2, c("lnV", "lnCL")] / expected[1:2, ] - 1) < 0.1),   # linearisation confirmed (A, B)
  abs(simulated[3, "lnV"] / expected[3, "lnV"] - 1) < 0.1,                  # and for V in design C
  all(is.infinite(expected[4, ])),                                          # design D is not identifiable
  expected[1, "lnV"] < expected[2, "lnV"], expected[1, "lnCL"] < expected[3, "lnCL"])
```
:::


In design C, 19.6% of the virtual repetitions give a rising instead of a
falling line, so no valid clearance can be computed; the simulated standard error of CL is then not meaningful
beyond "very large".

### Step 5: the model-free baseline


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
set.seed(15152)
t_rich <- c(0.25, 0.5, 1, 2, 3, 4, 6, 8, 12)                       # nine samples (h)
c_rich <- conc_analytic(t_rich) * exp(rnorm(length(t_rich), 0, sigma_log))
terminal <- coef(lm(log(c_rich) ~ t_rich, subset = t_rich >= 4))   # log-linear terminal phase
k_terminal <- -unname(terminal[2])
c0_back <- exp(unname(coef(lm(log(c_rich[1:2]) ~ t_rich[1:2]))[1])) # back-extrapolated C at t = 0
auc_obs <- (c0_back + c_rich[1]) / 2 * t_rich[1] +
  sum(diff(t_rich) * (head(c_rich, -1) + tail(c_rich, -1)) / 2)    # trapezoidal rule
auc_inf <- auc_obs + tail(c_rich, 1) / k_terminal                  # extrapolated tail
CL_nca <- dose_mg / auc_inf
fit_model <- nls(log(c_rich) ~ log(dose_mg) - lnV - exp(lnCL - lnV) * t_rich,
                 start = list(lnV = log(15), lnCL = log(4)))
model_est <- exp(coef(fit_model))
c(CL_nca = CL_nca, CL_model = unname(model_est["lnCL"]), V_model = unname(model_est["lnV"]),
  share_auc_extrapolated = (auc_inf - auc_obs) / auc_inf)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
#>                 CL_nca               CL_model                V_model 
#>             5.36968529             5.48494089            22.02396286 
#> share_auc_extrapolated 
#>             0.04612253
```


:::

```{.r .cell-code}
stopifnot(abs(CL_nca / CL_l_h - 1) < 0.15, abs(model_est[["lnCL"]] / CL_l_h - 1) < 0.15)
```
:::


With nine samples, the baseline and the model agree with the virtual clearance within the error to be expected from
a single person (NCA 5.37 L/h, model 5.48 L/h, virtual
value 5 L/h). The baseline needs no structural assumption, but it needs rich sampling; the two-sample designs of the
case need the model.

### Step 6: interindividual variability and the two-stage shortcut

Virtual persons now differ: ln CL and ln V vary with a standard deviation of 0.3 (*assumption*). A two-stage
analysis estimates each person's parameters from their two samples and then summarises the spread. The spread of
the individual estimates mixes true variability and estimation error.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
set.seed(15153)
n_persons <- 200
omega <- 0.3                                                         # between-person SD on the log scale
persons <- data.frame(V = V_l * exp(rnorm(n_persons, 0, omega)), CL = CL_l_h * exp(rnorm(n_persons, 0, omega)))
two_stage_sd <- function(t1, t2) {
  y1 <- log(conc_analytic(t1, V = persons$V, CL = persons$CL)) + rnorm(n_persons, 0, sigma_log)
  y2 <- log(conc_analytic(t2, V = persons$V, CL = persons$CL)) + rnorm(n_persons, 0, sigma_log)
  k_hat <- (y1 - y2) / (t2 - t1)
  CL_hat <- k_hat * dose_mg / exp(y1 + k_hat * t1)
  ok <- CL_hat > 0                                                   # rising lines give no valid clearance
  c(sd_lnCL = sd(log(CL_hat[ok])), true_sd_lnCL = sd(log(persons$CL)), share_invalid = mean(!ok))
}
spread <- rbind(A = two_stage_sd(0.5, 8), B = two_stage_sd(6, 8))
round(spread, 3)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
#>   sd_lnCL true_sd_lnCL share_invalid
#> A   0.320        0.301             0
#> B   0.417        0.301             0
```


:::

```{.r .cell-code}
stopifnot(spread["B", "sd_lnCL"] > spread["A", "sd_lnCL"])          # imprecise design inflates the apparent variability
```
:::


With the late design B, the apparent between-person spread of the clearance is inflated more than with design A. A
population model estimates variability and error jointly and avoids this bias; in R it can be fitted with
`nlme::nlme()` or with dedicated pharmacometric software. Such models are the next step and are outside this chapter.

::: {.callout-note title="Other implementation: Julia/SciML and SciPy"}
**Julia/SciML.** DifferentialEquations.jl [@rackauckas2017diffeq] (version 8.1.1, August 2026;
[documentation](https://docs.sciml.ai/DiffEqDocs/stable/)) offers a large set of solvers behind one interface. Its
documentation recommends `Tsit5` for most non-stiff problems, Verner methods (`Vern7`, `Vern8`) when high accuracy is
needed, and Rosenbrock methods such as `Rodas5P` for stiff problems; the Fortran `lsoda` used by deSolve is available
through a wrapper. The concrete advantage for this chapter lies in sensitivities: SciMLSensitivity.jl
([documentation](https://docs.sciml.ai/SciMLSensitivity/stable/)) computes forward and adjoint sensitivities of the
solution with respect to the parameters by automatic differentiation. For the one-compartment model, Step 4 used the
closed-form sensitivities −1 + k·t and −k·t; for models without a closed-form solution, the same Fisher-information
argument needs numerical sensitivities, and this is where the ecosystem helps.

**SciPy.** `scipy.integrate.solve_ivp` (SciPy 1.18.1, August 2026;
[documentation](https://docs.scipy.org/doc/scipy/reference/generated/scipy.integrate.solve_ivp.html))
[@virtanen2020scipy] connects the model to existing Python data pipelines. Its default method is `RK45` with
rtol = 10^−3^ and atol = 10^−6^, looser than the deSolve defaults; `method="LSODA"` wraps the same ODEPACK solver
family.

**For a fair comparison**, all implementations need the same parameters and units (mg, L, h), the same initial state,
the same output times (`t_eval` in SciPy, `saveat` in Julia), the same reference (the analytical solution) and the
same pre-specified tolerance (relative deviation ≤ 10^−4^). Solver name and tolerances must be reported. Statements
about speed need a benchmark on the same machine. Status: conceptual comparison, not run.
:::

**If the result stays unclear.** If a design turns out not to separate CL and V – for example because samples were
taken later than planned – report that the volume is not identifiable from these data. Do not fix it silently. The
options are to add an early sample in the next participants (if the protocol allows), to fix V at a published value
and label it as an *assumption* with its source, or to borrow strength across participants in a population model.
Each option changes what the result means and belongs in the report.

## Counter-check {#sec-b15-countercheck}

Change one virtual parameter: the clearance is halved to 2.5 L/h, for example in people with reduced elimination;
the volume and the designs stay the same. **Predict first:** does the expected precision of the clearance improve or
worsen for the late design B? And for the volume?


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
expected_low_cl <- t(mapply(function(a, b) expected_se(c(a, b), CL = CL_l_h / 2), designs$t1, designs$t2))
counter <- data.frame(Design = design_table$Design,
                      `CL expected, CL = 5` = pct(expected[, "lnCL"]),
                      `CL expected, CL = 2.5` = pct(expected_low_cl[, "lnCL"]),
                      `V expected, CL = 5` = pct(expected[, "lnV"]),
                      `V expected, CL = 2.5` = pct(expected_low_cl[, "lnV"]),
                      check.names = FALSE)
counter
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
#>               Design CL expected, CL = 5 CL expected, CL = 2.5
#> 1  A: early and late                   7                    10
#> 2       B: both late                  22                    10
#> 3      C: both early                  92                   205
#> 4 D: same time twice    not identifiable      not identifiable
#>   V expected, CL = 5 V expected, CL = 2.5
#> 1                 11                   11
#> 2                 50                   50
#> 3                 22                   22
#> 4   not identifiable     not identifiable
```


:::

```{.r .cell-code}
stopifnot(expected_low_cl[2, "lnCL"] < expected[2, "lnCL"],                    # design B improves for CL
          isTRUE(all.equal(expected_low_cl[1:3, "lnV"], expected[1:3, "lnV"])), # V precision unchanged
          expected_low_cl[3, "lnCL"] > expected[3, "lnCL"])                     # design C worsens for CL
```
:::


With the lower clearance, the late design B estimates the clearance more precisely
(22% → 10%), because the samples now lie closer to the
time V / CL = 8 h at which a sample is informative about CL only. The early design C gets worse. The precision of the
volume does not change at all: on the log scale, the intercept's uncertainty depends only on the sampling times. The
practical lesson is that a sampling schedule tuned to one assumed clearance may be poor for patients who differ
from it. Protocols for heterogeneous populations therefore spread sampling times or allow windows.

## Consequences for patients and operations {#sec-b15-consequences}

**Patients and ethics.** Every sample is a needle, a volume of blood and often a disturbed night; in critically ill
or young patients the volume matters. A design that is identifiable with two samples is a direct benefit, and a
design that wastes samples on times that carry little information is a harm without return. The protocol should
state why each sampling time is needed.

**Regulation.** A model fitted for a research question is not a product. Software that calculates an individual dose
from measured concentrations for use in patient care has a medical purpose, and its classification has to be
examined (@sec-b22). The virtual parameters here must never be used for such a calculation.

**Data protection and security.** Concentration–time data with dosing times, body weight and laboratory values are
health data. Sharing them for re-analysis needs pseudonymisation and controlled access (@sec-b23, @sec-b26). The model
code, solver settings and the tolerance check belong under version control, so that a later re-analysis uses the same
numerical method (@sec-b04).

## Look up and transfer {#sec-b15-lookup}

**Reviewer question.** Were the sampling times chosen so that each reported parameter is identifiable, and do the
reported standard errors account for the design – or were some parameters fixed without saying so?

**Self-test.** A virtual compound is given as an intravenous bolus, and only the AUC (from many samples) is reported
for each person. Which of CL and V can be estimated, and why?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Answer"}
Only the clearance: AUC = dose / CL, so CL = dose / AUC. The volume does not appear in the AUC at all; parameter sets
with the same CL and any V give the same AUC. V is structurally non-identifiable from the AUC alone; it needs the
shape of the curve, for example an early concentration or the terminal slope.
:::
